dedupe_keys.name: dtalite and nexta with the path4gmns python interface

description: DTALite is an open-source analysis, modelling and simulation library for fast macroscopic and mesoscopic traffic assignment on networks in the General Modeling Network Specification (GMNS) format. Its queue-based mesoscopic simulator, described by Zhou and Taylor in Cogent Engineering (2014) for fast model evaluation and calibration, loads origin-destination demand onto road and multimodal networks by static user-equilibrium assignment and then dynamic traffic assignment, with origin-destination demand estimation, space-time parallel computing and a simplified emission model among its documented extensions. NeXTA, developed with Federal Highway Administration support, visualises networks and traffic results, also through QGIS. The Python package Path4GMNS (version 0.10.0 of 16 December 2025 on PyPI, Apache 2.0) calls the C++ DTALite engine and adds shortest paths, link- and path-based equilibrium, accessibility and equity measures, and zone and demand synthesis. It is maintained by the Transportation AI Lab at Arizona State University. It is location independent and runs at corridor, city, regional and state scale; the README lists state-wide modelling in Maryland and work-zone analysis in North Carolina among uses. DTALite is free on GitHub under GPL-3.0 with a Windows release; the last commit was August 2024, and a redesign continues as TransOMS. Caveats: the Windows package and several forks make versions hard to follow, and some Path4GMNS versions could not call DTALite. DTALite supports network flow, capacity planning and work-zone disruption and resilience studies of road networks, and relates to the GMNS standard and to AequilibraE and MATSim, catalogued here.
